sternum.fact: Midline bone of the anterior chest; ribs connect to it through costal cartilage.

ribs.fact: Curved thoracic bones that protect the heart and lungs and articulate posteriorly with vertebrae.

pelvic girdle.fact: The paired hip bones form the pelvic girdle and connect the lower limbs to the axial skeleton.

clavicle.fact: An S-shaped bone connecting the sternum to the scapula at the shoulder girdle.

vertebral column.fact: A stack of vertebrae that supports the trunk and surrounds the spinal cord.

scapula.fact: A flat posterior shoulder bone that articulates with the humerus and clavicle.

sacrum.fact: A fused triangular bone at the base of the vertebral column between the hip bones.

coccyx.fact: Small terminal bone inferior to the sacrum; usually formed from fused coccygeal vertebrae.

humerus.fact: The single long bone of the arm, extending from shoulder to elbow.

radius.fact: Forearm bone on the lateral, thumb side in anatomical position; broader distally near the wrist.

ulna.fact: Forearm bone on the medial, pinky side in anatomical position; forms the prominent elbow with its olecranon.

carpals.fact: Eight bones form the wrist. As a group, carpals are taught as short bones; the pisiform is a sesamoid exception.

metacarpals.fact: Five bones of the palm lie between the carpals and finger phalanges.

hand phalanges.fact: The finger bones; most digits have proximal, middle, and distal phalanges.

femur.fact: The long bone of the thigh and the largest bone in the human body.

patella.fact: A sesamoid bone within the quadriceps tendon at the anterior knee.

tibia.fact: The larger, medial weight-bearing bone of the lower leg.

fibula.fact: The slender, lateral bone of the lower leg; it bears much less body weight than the tibia.

tarsals.fact: Seven short bones form the proximal foot, including the talus and calcaneus.

metatarsals.fact: Five long bones connect the tarsal region to the toe phalanges.

foot phalanges.fact: Bones of the toes; the great toe has two phalanges and the others usually have three.

frontal.fact: Forms the forehead and part of the superior orbit.

parietal.fact: Forms much of the superior and lateral cranial vault.

temporal.fact: Forms part of the lateral skull around the ear region and contributes to the jaw joint.

occipital.fact: Forms the posterior and inferior part of the cranium.

zygomatic.fact: Forms the prominence of the cheek and part of the lateral orbit.

maxilla.fact: Paired bone of the upper jaw that holds the upper teeth and contributes to the orbit.

mandible.fact: The movable lower jaw bone; it holds the lower teeth.

epiphysis.fact: An expanded end of a long bone. In the class model, the ends contain spongy bone covered by an outer layer of compact bone.

metaphysis.fact: Transition region between the shaft and an expanded end of a long bone.

diaphysis.fact: The central shaft of a long bone. It is mostly compact bone surrounding a central medullary canal.

compact bone.fact: Dense, cortical bone forms much of the shaft and the outer covering of the bone ends.

spongy bone.fact: Porous bone found inside the bone ends. Also called cancellous or trabecular bone; it contains red marrow, which produces blood cells.

medullary cavity.fact: The medullary cavity is the central space in the diaphysis; marrow is tissue within that space, not another name for the cavity.

yellow marrow.fact: Fatty tissue inside the central medullary canal of the shaft, important for fat storage.

periosteum.fact: A protective vascular membrane covering the non-articular exterior of the bone. It is not the lining of the central cavity; joint surfaces have articular cartilage.

blood vessel.fact: Blood vessels supply blood to the bone. The class slideshow identifies nutrient arteries as the blood supply to the shaft.

articular cartilage.fact: Hyaline cartilage covers bone surfaces at joints, providing a smooth surface for movement.

epiphyseal plate.fact: The thin band labeled epiphyseal plate near each end in the class model. This edition identifies the structure only, not its growth-related changes.

vertebra.fact: An individual bone of the spine. Its body, arch, and processes support the trunk, protect the spinal cord, and provide attachment sites.

true ribs.fact: Pairs 1-7 attach to the sternum through their own costal cartilages.

indirect ribs.fact: Pairs 8-10 reach the sternum indirectly through the cartilage of the rib above. They are false ribs but not floating ribs.

floating ribs.fact: Pairs 11-12 articulate posteriorly with vertebrae but have no attachment to the sternum. They are a subset of false ribs.

manubrium.fact: The broad superior part of the sternum articulates with the clavicles.

sternal body.fact: The elongated middle part of the sternum lies between the manubrium and xiphoid process.

xiphoid process.fact: The small inferior part of the sternum lies below its body.

cervical.fact: Seven cervical vertebrae form the neck region, superior to the thoracic region.

thoracic.fact: Twelve thoracic vertebrae form the rib-bearing region of the vertebral column.

lumbar.fact: Five lumbar vertebrae form the lower back, between the thoracic region and sacrum.

sacral.fact: Five vertebrae fuse to form the sacrum, between the hip bones and superior to the coccyx.

coccygeal.fact: Usually four small vertebrae fuse to form the coccyx at the inferior end of the column. The number can vary.

intervertebral discs.fact: Fibrocartilaginous discs between adjacent vertebral bodies help distribute loads and permit limited movement. There is no disc between C1 and C2.

sphenoid.fact: A cranial bone contributing to the base of the skull and the orbit; its greater wing is visible behind the orbit in this lateral view.

sutures.fact: Fibrous joints join most skull bones; their interlocking boundaries are not normal fracture lines.

red marrow.fact: Red bone marrow produces blood cells. The class model places it within spongy bone.
